items.title: CIDR cheat table
items.description: Prefix, subnet mask and usable hosts (2^(32-prefix) minus 2).

items.title: Subnet calculation method
items.body:
1. Block size = 256 - (interesting octet of the mask)   e.g. /27 -> 256 - 224 = 32
2. Network = largest multiple of the block size <= the address octet
3. Broadcast = network + block size - 1
4. Hosts = network + 1 ... broadcast - 1
items.description: Find network, broadcast and host range for any address.

items.title: Worked example: 192.168.5.77/27
items.body:
Mask: 255.255.255.224   Block size: 32
Network:   192.168.5.64     (64 is the largest multiple of 32 that is <= 77)
Broadcast: 192.168.5.95
Usable:    192.168.5.65 - 192.168.5.94   (30 hosts)

items.title: Worked example: split a /24 into four /26
items.body:
192.168.10.0/26    hosts .1   - .62    broadcast .63
192.168.10.64/26   hosts .65  - .126   broadcast .127
192.168.10.128/26  hosts .129 - .190   broadcast .191
192.168.10.192/26  hosts .193 - .254   broadcast .255
(Each extra bit borrowed from the host part doubles the subnets and halves the hosts.)

items.title: How many subnets and hosts
items.body:
Subnets created by borrowing n bits: 2^n
Hosts per subnet with h host bits:   2^h - 2
Total addresses in a /p block:       2^(32 - p)
Example: /22 has 2^10 = 1024 addresses (10.0.0.0/22 = 10.0.0.0 - 10.0.3.255)

items.title: OSI model layers
items.body:
7 Application   HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH
6 Presentation  TLS, encoding, compression
5 Session       sessions, RPC
4 Transport     TCP, UDP (ports)
3 Network       IP, ICMP, routing (routers)
2 Data link     Ethernet, Wi-Fi, MAC addresses (switches)
1 Physical      cables, radio, bits
Mnemonic (7 to 1): All People Seem To Need Data Processing

items.title: TCP vs UDP
items.body:
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, congestion control (web, SSH, email, databases)
UDP: connectionless, no delivery guarantee, low latency (DNS, VoIP, video, games)
TCP handshake: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK

items.title: DNS record types
items.body:
A      name -> IPv4 address            AAAA   name -> IPv6 address
CNAME  alias -> another name           MX     mail servers (with priority)
TXT    free text (SPF, verification)   NS     authoritative name servers
PTR    IP -> name (reverse lookup)     SOA    zone authority information
SRV    service host and port

items.title: ip: addresses, links and routes
items.body:
ip a
ip -br a                    # brief
ip link
ip route
ip route get 8.8.8.8        # which route/interface is used
items.description: Modern replacement for ifconfig and route.

items.title: ip: change addresses (temporary)
items.body:
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0
sudo ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1

items.title: ss: sockets and listening ports
items.body:
ss -tulpn            # listening TCP/UDP with process (needs sudo for others' processes)
ss -tn state established
ss -s                # summary
ss -tn dst :443

items.title: dig: DNS queries
items.body:
dig example.com
dig +short example.com A
dig example.com MX
dig example.com TXT
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com        # ask a specific resolver
dig -x 8.8.8.8                  # reverse lookup
dig +trace example.com
items.description: Look up records and test resolvers.

items.title: traceroute and mtr
items.body:
traceroute example.com
traceroute -n example.com       # no reverse DNS, faster
mtr -rw example.com             # report mode, wide
items.description: See the path packets take and where latency or loss starts.

items.title: ping and port checks
items.body:
ping -c 4 example.com
nc -zv example.com 443          # is the port open?
curl -v telnet://example.com:25 --connect-timeout 5
items.description: Reachability, then a specific TCP port.

items.title: tcpdump basics
items.body:
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80
sudo tcpdump -i any host 192.168.1.10 -nn
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap       # open in Wireshark
items.description: Capture traffic (needs root; use responsibly on your own network).

items.title: Routing table basics
items.body:
1. Match the destination against the routing table (longest prefix wins).
2. Directly connected network -> deliver on the local link (ARP for the MAC).
3. Otherwise send to the default gateway (0.0.0.0/0).
Check with:  ip route    and    ip route get <destination>
items.description: How a host decides where to send a packet.
